Fix a trial \(e\), a covariate value \(x\), and a proxy value \(z\).  The conditioning event has positive probability by observed-cell positivity.  Put \(\bar g_e(w,x)=g_{r_e}(w,x)-g_{l_e}(w,x)\).  Balanced randomization and consistency give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_Q[\widetilde Y_e\mid Z_e=z,X=x,S=e]
&=\mathbb E_Q[Y(r_e)-Y(l_e)\mid Z_e=z,X=x,S=e].
\end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, conditional on all baseline variables and \(Y_a\), each treatment arm has probability \(1/2\), and the factor \(2\) in \(\widetilde Y_e\) cancels that probability.  Let \(H^Q_{e,x}[z,u]=Q(U=u\mid Z_e=z,X=x,S=e)\).  Successive conditioning, proxy exclusion, and the shared-contrast bridge imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_Q[Y(r_e)-Y(l_e)\mid z,x,e]
&=\sum_u H^Q_{e,x}[z,u]
  \mathbb E_Q[Y(r_e)-Y(l_e)\mid x,u,e]\\
&=\sum_{u,w}H^Q_{e,x}[z,u]C_x(w\mid u)\bar g_e(w,x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Common-proxy invariance and proxy exclusion also give, entry by entry,
\[
T_{e,x}[z,w]=\sum_u H^Q_{e,x}[z,u]C_x(w\mid u).
\]
Consequently
\[
\mathbb E_Q[\widetilde Y_e\mid z,x,e]
=\sum_wT_{e,x}[z,w]\bar g_e(w,x),
\]
which is precisely the \((e,x,z)\)-row of \(A_Pg=b_P\), by the definition of the reduced incidence row \(B_e\).  Stacking proves \(A_Pg=b_P\).

For the target population, the tower property and the shared-contrast bridge give, for \(a=1,\ldots,k\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\theta_a
&=\sum_{x,u}Q(x,u\mid S=0)
  \mathbb E_Q[Y(a)-Y(0)\mid x,u,S=0]\\
&=\sum_{x,u,w}Q(x,u\mid S=0)C_x(w\mid u)g_a(w,x)\\
&=\sum_{x,w}P(X=x,W=w\mid S=0)g_a(w,x)
=(R_0g)_a,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the penultimate equality uses the common \(W\)-given-\((X,U)\) kernel.  Thus \(\theta=R_0g\).  Since the model assumption supplies this \(g\), it is an element of \(H(P)\), and \(H(P)\ne\varnothing\).

Fix \(h\in\ker(A_P)\).  For every \(s,x,u,w\), the definition of \(d^h\) gives \(d^h_{s,a_s}(x,u,w)=0\); hence the vector \(d^h_s(x,u,w)=(d^h_{s,a}(x,u,w))_{a=0}^k\) belongs to \(D_{a_s}\).  The support-tangent assumption and the defining right-inverse identity for \(\Gamma_{s,x,u,w,a_s}\) therefore yield
\[
\operatorname{supp}(\Delta^h_{s,x,u,w})\subseteq\mathcal Y^+_{s,x,u,w},\qquad
\sum_y\Delta^h_{s,x,u,w}(y)=0,
\]
and, for every \(a\in V\),
\[
\sum_y\Delta^h_{s,x,u,w}(y)y_a=d^h_{s,a}(x,u,w).
\tag{1}
\]
All index sets are finite.  If \(\Delta^h\) is nonzero, each ratio entering \(\varepsilon_*(h)\) has a strictly positive numerator by the definition of \(\mathcal Y^+\), and there are finitely many ratios.  Thus \(\varepsilon_*(h)>0\).  If \(\Delta^h=0\), the empty-minimum convention gives \(\varepsilon_*(h)=+\infty\).  For \(|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_*(h)\), every changed coordinate satisfies
\[
K_{s,x,u,w}(y)+\varepsilon\Delta^h_{s,x,u,w}(y)
\ge K_{s,x,u,w}(y)-|\varepsilon|\,|\Delta^h_{s,x,u,w}(y)|>0.
\]
Coordinates outside the original positive support remain zero, and the zero-total-mass identity shows that each perturbed kernel is normalized.  Hence these kernels define a full-data law on the same finite latent and outcome supports.

We next prove preservation of the complete observed trial laws.  From \(A_Ph=0\), its \((e,x,z)\)-coordinate is
\[
0=\sum_wT_{e,x}[z,w]\{h_{r_e}(w,x)-h_{l_e}(w,x)\}
=\sum_uH^Q_{e,x}[z,u]\{r^h_{r_e}(x,u)-r^h_{l_e}(x,u)\},
\tag{2}
\]
where the factorization \(T_{e,x}=H^Q_{e,x}C_x\) follows from common-proxy invariance and proxy exclusion.  Under the perturbation, (1) says that the conditional probability of \(Y(a)=1\), given \((s,x,u,w)\), changes by \(\varepsilon d^h_{s,a}(x,u,w)\); because total mass is unchanged and the outcome is binary, the probability of \(Y(a)=0\) changes by its negative.  For the left endpoint of trial \(e\), \(d^h_{e,l_e}=0\), so every observed left-arm cell is unchanged.  For the right endpoint and \(y\in\{0,1\}\), the change in the conditional \((W=w,Y=y)\) cell given \((Z_e=z,X=x,S=e,A=r_e)\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\varepsilon(2y-1)\sum_uH^Q_{e,x}[z,u]C_x(w\mid u)d^h_{e,r_e}(x,u,w)\\
&\quad=\varepsilon(2y-1)\rho_x(w)
\sum_uH^Q_{e,x}[z,u]\{r^h_{r_e}(x,u)-r^h_{l_e}(x,u)\}=0
\end{aligned}
\]
by (2).  Randomization probabilities and the \((X,Z_e,W)\) margins are fixed, so this proves equality of every complete observed trial cell.  The target records only \((X,W)\), whose law was not changed.  The new outcome kernel still does not depend on \(Z_e\) conditional on \((X,U,W,S=e)\); thus proxy exclusion is retained.  Assignment, the latent mixing laws, all proxy kernels, latent support, and the observed \(\eta\)-positivity restriction are retained because they are fixed or because the observed law is exactly \(P\).  The all-edges-incomplete restriction is also retained because every \(T_{e,x}\) is unchanged.

It remains to verify the shared latent contrast restriction.  Strict positivity of \(C_x(w\mid u)\) justifies the division in \(d^h\), and \(\sum_w\rho_x(w)=1\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_wC_x(w\mid u)\{d^h_{s,a}(x,u,w)-d^h_{s,0}(x,u,w)\}
&=r^h_a(x,u)-r^h_0(x,u)\\
&=r^h_a(x,u)\\
&=\sum_wC_x(w\mid u)h_a(w,x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore the treatment-\(a\) versus treatment-\(0\) conditional mean under \(Q^{\varepsilon,h}\) equals its value under \(Q\) plus \(\varepsilon C_xh_a\).  Since \(g\) is a bridge under \(Q\), \(g+\varepsilon h\) is a bridge under \(Q^{\varepsilon,h}\), simultaneously for every population and node.  Finally, applying the target calculation in the observable-reduction lemma to the bridge increment yields
\[
\theta(Q^{\varepsilon,h})-\theta(Q)=\varepsilon R_0h.
\]
Every defining member property of \(\mathcal M_{L,\eta}\) has now been checked, proving the claim.

Let \(N=kd|\mathcal X|\), the number of columns of \(A_P\).  By rank--nullity,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{rank}([A_P;R_0])-\operatorname{rank}(A_P)
&=\{N-\dim(\ker A_P\cap\ker R_0)\}
  -\{N-\dim\ker A_P\}\\
&=\dim\ker A_P-\dim(\ker A_P\cap\ker R_0)\\
&=\dim(R_0\ker A_P).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
Thus \(\nu(P)=0\) if and only if \(\ker(A_P)\subseteq\ker(R_0)\).

Assume first that this inclusion holds.  For any two compatible full-data laws, the observable-reduction lemma supplies bridges \(g_1,g_2\in H(P)\) and targets \(R_0g_1,R_0g_2\).  Since \(A_P(g_1-g_2)=0\), the inclusion gives \(R_0(g_1-g_2)=0\).  Hence their targets agree, so \(\theta\) is point identified.

Conversely, if the inclusion fails, choose \(h\in\ker(A_P)\) with \(R_0h\ne0\), and choose any compatible completion \(Q\), which exists by compatibility.  The signed-cell lift provides a positive radius and, for any \(0<|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_*(h)\), another compatible completion with the same \(P\) and target \(\theta(Q)+\varepsilon R_0h\ne\theta(Q)\).  Thus point identification fails.  This proves the first equivalence without replacing causal compatibility by the bridge equation.

Finite-dimensional row--nullspace duality gives
\[
\ker(A_P)\subseteq\ker(R_0)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{row}(R_0)\subseteq\operatorname{row}(A_P).
\tag{2}
\]
For completeness, the forward implication follows because every row of \(R_0\) annihilates \(\ker(A_P)\), whose orthogonal complement is \(\operatorname{row}(A_P)\); the reverse implication is immediate.  The row inclusion in (2) holds exactly when every row of \(R_0\) is a linear combination of the rows of \(A_P\), that is, exactly when a matrix \(F_P\) exists with \(F_PA_P=R_0\).  In that event the observable-reduction identity gives
\[
\theta=R_0g=F_PA_Pg=F_Pb_P.
\]
The cited statistical-annihilator result records that Proposition 2.3 of \cite{ZhangLiMiaoTchetgen2023} concerns invariance of a functional over solutions of an operator equation.  The necessity argument above additionally realizes every violating direction by full finite causal completions preserving the entire observed network law.  Forgetting those completions leaves exactly the statistical criterion, establishing the stated comparison.

Let \(\nu=\nu(P)=\dim(R_0\ker A_P)\).  If \(\nu=0\), the asserted relative neighborhood is the singleton \(\{\theta(Q)\}\) in a zero-dimensional affine space.  Suppose \(\nu>0\).  Choose \(h_1,\ldots,h_\nu\in\ker(A_P)\) so that \(R_0h_1,\ldots,R_0h_\nu\) form a basis of \(R_0\ker(A_P)\), and let \(\Delta_j\) be the signed-cell array produced from \(h_j\).  The maps \(h\mapsto r^h\), \(r^h\mapsto d^h\), and \(d^h\mapsto\Gamma d^h\) are linear; hence the array for \(\sum_jt_jh_j\) is \(\sum_jt_j\Delta_j\).

On the finite positive support define
\[
M=\max_{s,x,u,w,y:\,K_{s,x,u,w}(y)>0}
\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}|\Delta_{j,s,x,u,w}(y)|}{K_{s,x,u,w}(y)}.
\]
Here \(0<M<\infty\): finiteness and positivity give finiteness, while \(M=0\) would imply every \(\Delta_j=0\), and the bridge calculation in the signed-cell proof would then imply \(R_0h_j=0\), contradicting the chosen basis.  If \(\|t\|_\infty<M^{-1}\), then
\[
\left|\sum_jt_j\Delta_{j,s,x,u,w}(y)\right|
\le\|t\|_\infty\sum_j|\Delta_{j,s,x,u,w}(y)|
<K_{s,x,u,w}(y)
\]
on every positive atom.  The same linear preservation equations used in the signed-cell theorem show that replacing \(K\) by \(K+\sum_jt_j\Delta_j\) gives a compatible law with observed law \(P\) and target
\[
\theta(Q)+\sum_{j=1}^{\nu}t_jR_0h_j.
\]
As \(t\) ranges over the open cube \(\|t\|_\infty<M^{-1}\), these targets form a relatively open neighborhood of \(\theta(Q)\) in \(\theta(Q)+R_0\ker(A_P)\).  Its dimension is \(\nu\) by (1) in the exact-nullity proof.

Fix \(e,x,z,w\).  The tower property, proxy exclusion, and the common proxy kernel give
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{e,x}[z,w]
&=\sum_uQ(U=u\mid Z_e=z,X=x,S=e)
 Q(W=w\mid Z_e=z,X=x,U=u,S=e)\\
&=\sum_uH^Q_{e,x}[z,u]C_x(w\mid u).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(T_{e,x}=H^Q_{e,x}C_x\).  With \(\widetilde A_x=\operatorname{stack}_{e\in E}(B_e\otimes H^Q_{e,x})\), the mixed-product identity for Kronecker products yields
\[
A_{P,x}=\widetilde A_x(I_{|V|-1}\otimes C_x).
\]
Therefore
\[
\operatorname{rank}(A_{P,x})
\le\operatorname{rank}(I_{|V|-1}\otimes C_x)
=q_x(|V|-1).
\]
Because \(C_x\) has \(|\mathcal U|\) rows and \(d\) columns,
\(q_x\le\min\{|\mathcal U|,d\}\le\min\{L,d\}\).  Finally, \(A_P\) is block diagonal over \(x\), so
\[
\operatorname{rank}(A_P)=\sum_x\operatorname{rank}(A_{P,x})
\le(|V|-1)\sum_xq_x.
\]

Write \(k=|V|-1\) and suppress the fixed \(x\).  Every row \(c_u=C_x(u,\cdot)\) is stochastic, so the coordinate-sum functional \(\ell(t)=\sum_wt_w\) equals \(1\) on every \(c_u\).  If \(S_C=\operatorname{span}\{c_u:u\in\mathcal U\}\), then \(\dim S_C=q\), while
\[
H_C=\operatorname{aff}\{c_u\}=\{t\in S_C:\ell(t)=1\}
\]
has dimension \(q-1\).  Indeed, after fixing one row \(c_{u_0}\), the row differences span a \((q-1)\)-dimensional subspace contained in \(\ker\ell\), and \(c_{u_0}\notin\ker\ell\).

We verify that the stochastic attainability restriction does not reduce this affine dimension.  Choose \(\pi_*\in D_C(\eta_0)\), which exists by hypothesis.  All inequalities in the definition of \(D_C(\eta_0)\) are strict, so every sufficiently small \(v\) with \(\sum_uv_u=0\) has \(\pi_*+v\in D_C(\eta_0)\).  The linear map \(v\mapsto v^{\mathsf T}C_x\) maps the subspace \(\sum_uv_u=0\) onto \(H_C-H_C\), because the row differences span the latter space.  A linear surjection between finite-dimensional spaces maps a neighborhood of zero onto a neighborhood of zero: choose preimages of a basis and use the resulting linear right inverse.  Hence \(O_C(\eta_0)\) is a nonempty relatively open subset of \(H_C\), and its affine hull is \(H_C\).

Choose linear coordinates on \(S_C\) in which \(\ell\) is the first coordinate, and extend them to an invertible linear coordinate change on \(\mathbb R^d\).  Then each attainable row has coordinates
\[
t_e=(1,p_{e1},\ldots,p_{e,q-1},0,\ldots,0).
\]
All rows of \(T_{e,x}\) are copies of \(t_e\), so deleting duplicate rows does not change rank.  After the corresponding invertible column transformation, the nonzero part of \(A_{P,x}\) is
\[
\mathcal A(p)=
\bigl[B,\ \operatorname{diag}(p_{\cdot1})B,\ \ldots,
\operatorname{diag}(p_{\cdot,q-1})B\bigr],
\tag{1}
\]
where \(B\) is the reduced incidence matrix with rows \(B_e\).  The remaining \(k(d-q)\) columns are zero.

We use the elementary incidence fact that a \(k\)-row square submatrix \(B_F\) has nonzero determinant exactly when \(F\) is a spanning tree.  If \(F\) is a tree, orienting it away from the root and ordering each nonroot vertex after its parent makes \(B_F\) triangular up to row signs and permutations, with diagonal entries \(\pm1\).  If \(F\) contains a cycle, its incidence rows are dependent; if it is disconnected, the indicator of a root-free component gives a nonzero vector in the nullspace of \(B_F\).  These exhaust the non-tree cases with \(k\) edges.

Select \(qk\) edge rows in (1) and expand the corresponding determinant by its \(q\) column blocks.  Every nonzero term partitions the selected labeled edges into \(q\) sets \(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}\), each of size \(k\), and has coefficient
\[
\pm\prod_{j=0}^{q-1}\det(B_{F_j})
\]
times the monomial \(\prod_{j=1}^{q-1}\prod_{e\in F_j}p_{ej}\).  Distinct labeled partitions give distinct monomials: the variables in the monomial determine \(F_1,\ldots,F_{q-1}\), and the complement determines \(F_0\).  Thus cancellation between different partitions is impossible.  By the incidence fact, a nonzero determinant polynomial exists if and only if the graph contains \(q\) pairwise edge-disjoint spanning trees.

If there is no such packing, every \(qk\)-minor vanishes identically, while the proxy-rank ceiling gives rank at most \(qk\); hence the rank is always below \(qk\).  If there is a packing, its union supplies a \(qk\)-minor that is a nonzero polynomial in the relative coordinates \(p_{ej}\).  A nonzero real polynomial has a Lebesgue-null zero set.  This last fact follows by induction on the number of variables: write the polynomial as a polynomial in the last variable; outside the common zero set of its coefficient polynomials, each one-dimensional section has finitely many roots, and the induction hypothesis together with Fubini's theorem gives measure zero.  Since \(O_C(\eta_0)^E\) is relatively open in \(H_C^E\), the deficient collections are therefore the common zero set of the maximal minors and have \(\mu_C\)-measure zero.  When \(q=1\), there are no relative coordinates and (1) is \(B\); connectedness gives rank \(k\), agreeing with the zero-dimensional point-mass convention.

For finitely many covariate strata, block diagonality gives
\(\operatorname{rank}(A_P)=\sum_x\operatorname{rank}(A_{P,x})\).  Taking the finite product of the stratumwise relative measures, the intersection of the almost-sure full-rank events has probability one.  Hence the generic global rank is \(\sum_xq_x(|V|-1)\) exactly under the stated tree-packing condition in every stratum.

The cited matroid-union rank theorem states that the rank of the union of \(q\) copies of a matroid with rank function \(r_M\), on ground set \(E\), is
\[
\min_{F\subseteq E}\{|E\setminus F|+q\,r_M(F)\}.
\tag{1}
\]
For the graphic matroid of the spanning multigraph \((V,E)\), a maximal forest in \((V,F)\) has one fewer edge than vertices in each component, and hence
\[
r_M(F)=\sum_{j=1}^{c(F)}(|V_j|-1)=|V|-c(F).
\tag{2}
\]
The independent sets of the union are precisely edge sets partitionable into \(q\) pairwise disjoint forests, so its rank on \(E\) is the defined quantity \(r_q(E)\).  Substituting (2) into (1) proves
\[
r_q(E)=\min_{F\subseteq E}
\{|E\setminus F|+q(|V|-c(F))\}.
\]
Moreover, \(r_q(E)=q(|V|-1)\) if and only if the maximizing forest family consists of \(q\) forests each having \(|V|-1\) edges, hence of \(q\) spanning trees.  This is also the tree-packing condition characterized by the cited Nash--Williams partition theorem.  The forest family certifies the lower bound, and a minimizing \(F\) in the display certifies the matching upper bound.  Combining this classical certificate with the generic-tree-rank theorem gives exactly the claimed causal-operator certificate; the min--max identity itself remains the cited classical result.

The feasible family in the definition of \(F_*\) is a finite nonempty collection of subsets of \(E^+\), and every cost is positive, so a minimum-cost member exists.  For such a member,
\[
r_q(E\cup F_*)=q(|V|-1).
\]
The matroid corollary then gives \(q\) edge-disjoint spanning trees in \(E\cup F_*\), and the generic-tree-rank theorem gives \(\operatorname{rank}(A_{P,x})=q(|V|-1)\) for almost every attainable row collection.

We next connect effective-rank saturation to target identification.  For a compatible target population,
\[
P(X=x,W=\cdot\mid S=0)
=P(X=x\mid S=0)\pi_{0,x}^{\mathsf T}C_x
\in\operatorname{row}(C_x).
\tag{1}
\]
The factorization in the proxy-rank proof shows
\[
\operatorname{row}(A_{P,x})
\subseteq\operatorname{row}(I_{|V|-1}\otimes C_x),
\]
and the space on the right has dimension \(q_x(|V|-1)\).  If saturation holds, equality of dimensions makes the two row spaces equal.  By (1), every \(x\)-block of every row of \(R_0\) lies in this common row space.  If saturation holds in every stratum, \(\operatorname{row}(R_0)\subseteq\operatorname{row}(A_P)\), equivalently \(\ker(A_P)\subseteq\ker(R_0)\).  The exact-nullity theorem then identifies every root contrast, for any compatible target mixture \(\pi_{0,x}\).

Adding one labeled element to a matroid increases rank by at most one.  Iterating gives
\[
r_q(E\cup F)\le r_q(E)+|F|.
\]
Thus every saturating augmentation satisfies
\[
|F|\ge q(|V|-1)-r_q(E).
\]
If the menu contains an extension \(F\) of a maximum union-independent subset of \(E\) to a union basis of size \(q(|V|-1)\), then \(|F|\) equals this deficit and equality is attained.  Finally, if the menu contains no saturating \(F\), the matroid rank remains below \(q(|V|-1)\) for every permitted augmentation; the generic-tree-rank theorem then precludes removal of that effective causal-operator rank deficit by any menu choice.

At \(x_1\), the mixture for the \(j\)-th ordered edge is \((j/8,1-j/8)\), so its attainable row is
\[
t_j=\left(\frac{4+j}{16},\frac{12-j}{16}\right),\qquad j=1,\ldots,6.
\tag{1}
\]
After omitting edge \(13\), multiply the five-row effective matrix by \(16\).  In node-by-proxy column order it is
\[
16A_{P,x_1}^{(5)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
5&11&0&0&0&0\\
-6&-10&6&10&0&0\\
0&0&-7&-9&7&9\\
0&0&8&8&0&0\\
0&0&0&0&9&7
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{2}
\]
The minor obtained by deleting the first column has determinant \(-11/1024\) before the scaling in (2), so the rank is \(5\).  Direct multiplication of (2) by
\[
h=(44,-20,-16,16,-7,9)^{\mathsf T}
\]
gives zero.  The target \(x_1\)-row is \((11/16,5/16)\), the target assigns probability \(1/2\) to \(x_1\), and \(h=0\) at \(x_2\).  Hence
\[
R_0h=\frac1{32}
\begin{pmatrix}
11(44)+5(-20)\\
11(-16)+5(16)\\
11(-7)+5(9)
\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}12\\-3\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{3}
\]

On the five positive outcome atoms, the displayed map \(\Gamma\) has total mass
\(-\sum_ad_a+\sum_ad_a=0\), and its \(a\)-th one-way marginal is \(d_a\).  It is therefore a right inverse for every \(d\in D_{a_s}\), so the support-tangent assumption holds despite the eleven structural-zero atoms.  The signed-cell theorem applied to (3) supplies a positive two-sided interval of laws with the same observed table and target increment \(\varepsilon(12,-3,-1)^{\mathsf T}\).

With edge \(13\), the two edge-disjoint spanning trees are
\[
\{01,12,23\}\quad\text{and}\quad\{02,03,13\}.
\]
Using \(t_6=(10/16,6/16)\), the determinant of the resulting \(6\)-by-\(6\) matrix is \(-21/4096\), so its actual rank at \(x_1\) is \(6\), as well as being the generic rank.  At \(x_2\), both rows of \(C_{x_2}\) equal \((1/2,1/2)\); all edge rows therefore have this common proxy factor, and the connected incidence matrix has rank \(3\).  Block diagonality gives global rank \(6+3=9\).  The target proxy row in each stratum belongs to the corresponding row space of \(C_x\), so the row-space argument in the augmentation proposition gives exact identification.  Nevertheless, at \(x_2\), \(q_{x_2}=1<d=2\), and the proxy-rank ceiling precludes recovery of all six \(W\)-indexed bridge coordinates in that stratum.

The three cited comparison-scope lemmas show respectively that the finite categorical result of \cite{MiaoGengTchetgen2018} uses full latent-rank proxy matrices, that the main indirect-comparison identification result of \cite{SuRytgaardRavnEriksson2026} is pairwise through a common comparator, and that \cite{DahabrehRobertsonPetitoHernanSteingrimsson2023} transports effects using observed modifiers.  The construction above has a rank-one proxy kernel at \(x_2\), a six-edge multigraph, and a latent modifier, proving the stated scope comparisons.

In one stratum the bridge has \(d(|V|-1)\) coordinates, so recovery of the full \(W\)-indexed bridge is equivalent to \(\ker(A_{P,x})=\{0\}\), or \(\operatorname{rank}(A_{P,x})=d(|V|-1)\).  The proxy-rank ceiling gives
\[
\operatorname{rank}(A_{P,x})\le q_x(|V|-1)\le d(|V|-1).
\]
Consequently full recovery requires \(q_x=d\).  If \(q_x=d\), the generic-tree-rank theorem says that generic rank equals \(d(|V|-1)\) exactly when \(\operatorname{TreePack}_d(G)\) holds.  This proves the equivalence.  If \(q_x<d\), the ceiling remains strict regardless of how many comparison edges are added, because adding edges does not change the fixed common-kernel rank.  On the other hand, exact target identification only requires \(R_0\ker(A_P)=\{0\}\), which can hold with a nonzero bridge nullspace, as asserted.

Use the corrected influence-function definitions based on the observable minimum weighted-norm representative \(g_*\).  Let \(p\) be the finite vector of primitive cell probabilities.  On the stated compact set, observed-cell positivity bounds every conditioning denominator away from zero; hence \(p\mapsto(A_P,b_P,R_0)\) is twice continuously differentiable with uniformly bounded derivatives.  The same is true of \(\Omega^{1/2}\), because \(\Omega\) is positive definite and twice continuously differentiable and compactness bounds its least eigenvalue away from zero.

Put \(M=M_P=\Omega^{1/2}A_P\), \(y=\Omega^{1/2}b_P\), and \(g_*=M^+y\).  Observable reduction gives \(b_P=A_Pg_*\), because \(y\in\operatorname{col}(M)\), and therefore \(Mg_*=y\).  Also
\[
M^+M=\Pi_{\operatorname{row}(A_P)},\qquad
R_0M^+M=R_0,
\tag{1}
\]
where the second identity follows from \(\ker(A_P)\subseteq\ker(R_0)\).

Uniform cell-frequency consistency and the singular-value perturbation bound in the cited separated-pseudoinverse lemma imply
\[
\sup_P\|\widehat M-M\|=O_P(n^{-1/2}).
\]
At the population matrix, \(\sigma_r(M)\ge\kappa\) and \(\sigma_{r+1}(M)=0\).  Thus, with probability tending to one uniformly, exactly \(r\) sample singular values exceed \(\kappa/2\).  On this event the truncated inverse is the smooth separated-rank extension covered by the cited lemma.

Differentiate \(\Phi(p)=R_0M^+y\).  For a matrix increment \(E=dM\), the cited derivative formula is
\[
D(M^+)[E]=-M^+EM^+
+M^+M^{+\mathsf T}E^{\mathsf T}(I-MM^+)
+(I-M^+M)E^{\mathsf T}M^{+\mathsf T}M^+.
\tag{2}
\]
Because \(y=Mg_*\), the middle term in (2), applied to \(y\), is zero.  The last term has range in \(\ker(M)=\ker(A_P)\), so left multiplication by \(R_0\) kills it.  Hence
\[
d\Phi=(dR_0)g_*+R_0M^+\{dy-(dM)g_*\}.
\]
Writing out \(M=\Omega^{1/2}A_P\) and \(y=\Omega^{1/2}b_P\), the derivatives of \(\Omega^{1/2}\) cancel because \(b_P-A_Pg_*=0\), and consequently
\[
d\Phi=(dR_0)g_*+R_0L_g\{db_P-(dA_P)g_*\}.
\tag{3}
\]
This calculation uses the unique \(g_*\) and nowhere requires uniqueness of solutions to \(A_Pg=b_P\).

For a trial observation, the quotient rule for the conditional moments in (3) gives
\[
v_e(O_e)[x,z]=
\frac{\mathbf 1\{X=x,Z_e=z\}}{P(X=x,Z_e=z\mid S=e)}
\left[\widetilde Y_e-\{g_{*,r_e}(W,X)-g_{*,l_e}(W,X)\}\right].
\]
The bracket has conditional mean zero by \(A_Pg_*=b_P\).  The derivative of the target integration map is
\[
\psi_0(O_0)=
(g_{*,1}(W,X),\ldots,g_{*,k}(W,X))^{\mathsf T}-\theta.
\]
Thus the finite-dimensional delta method and (3) give the uniform expansion
\[
\widehat\theta-\theta
=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S}\frac1{n_s}\sum_{i=1}^{n_s}\psi_s(O_{s,i})
+o_P(n^{-1/2}),
\tag{4}
\]
with \(\psi_e=R_0L_gJ_ev_e\).  The cited finite-multinomial central limit and delta-method result, positive limiting sampling fractions, and (4) yield
\[
\sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta)\ \Longrightarrow\
N_k(0,V(P,\lambda)),\qquad
V(P,\lambda)=\sum_s\lambda_s^{-1}\mathbb E_P[\psi_s\psi_s^{\mathsf T}].
\]
Uniformity follows because the supports are fixed and finite, all summands are uniformly bounded on the compact positive-cell set, and the derivatives and Taylor remainders above are uniformly bounded.  Equivalently, any contrary sequence has a convergent subsequence on which the ordinary finite-multinomial delta method gives the asserted limit.

The covariance is nonsingular.  If \(c^{\mathsf T}V(P,\lambda)c=0\), positivity of every \(\lambda_s\) implies \(c^{\mathsf T}\psi_e=0\) almost surely for every trial.  Let \(q_{e,x,z}\) be the \((x,z)\)-coordinate of \(c^{\mathsf T}R_0L_gJ_e\).  If it were nonzero, complete observed-cell positivity would give positive probability to both \(Y=0\) and \(Y=1\) in a fixed arm and \((x,z,w)\) cell, on which the bracket defining \(v_e\) takes two values differing by \(2\); it could not vanish almost surely.  Hence all \(q_{e,x,z}=0\), so \(c^{\mathsf T}R_0L_g=0\).  By (1),
\[
c^{\mathsf T}R_0=c^{\mathsf T}R_0L_gA_P=0.
\]
The rows of \(R_0\) are linearly independent because the positive target cell vector is nonzero and is placed in disjoint node blocks.  Therefore \(c=0\).  Continuity and compactness give a uniform positive lower bound on the least eigenvalue of \(V(P,\lambda)\).

Replacing the probabilities, \(g_*\), and influence-function moments by their empirical plug-in versions is uniformly consistent by the finite-support law of large numbers and the same separated smoothness.  Uniform Slutsky then gives convergence of the Wald quadratic form to \(\chi_k^2\), and the joint ellipsoid using its \(1-\alpha\) quantile has coverage converging uniformly to \(1-\alpha\).

For one complete cell with probability \(p\), its marginal count \(K\) is \(\operatorname{Binomial}(n,p)\), even though the full vector of counts is multinomial.  At the true \(p\), \(F_{n,K}(p)=\Pr_p\{X\le K\}\) is nondecreasing as a function of \(K\).  Hence the event \(F_{n,K}(p)<\delta/2\) is either empty or an initial segment \(\{0,\ldots,k_*\}\), and in the latter case
\[
\Pr_p\{F_{n,K}(p)<\delta/2\}=F_{n,k_*}(p)<\delta/2.
\]
Similarly, \(H_{n,K}(p)=\Pr_p\{X\ge K\}\) is nonincreasing in \(K\), so the event \(H_{n,K}(p)<\delta/2\) is empty or a terminal segment and has probability below \(\delta/2\).  Therefore, for every \(n\ge0\) and \(p\in[0,1]\),
\[
\Pr_p\{p\notin I_{n,K}(\delta)\}\le\delta.
\tag{1}
\]
When \(n=0\), both tail polynomials equal \(1\), so (1) also covers the zero-sample case; it likewise covers counts \(0\) and \(n\).

There are \(M_{\mathrm{total}}\) complete cells and \(\delta=\alpha/M_{\mathrm{total}}\).  Applying the union bound to (1), without requiring independence of cell counts, gives
\[
\Pr_P\{P\in B_n\}\ge1-M_{\mathrm{total}}\delta=1-\alpha.
\tag{2}
\]
On the event in (2), the true table also satisfies normalization, nonnegativity, the \(\eta\)-cell restriction, and the known randomization equalities; hence \(P\in\mathcal C_n^P\).  Fix any compatible full-data law \(Q\) with this observed law.  The observable-reduction lemma supplies its bridge \(g_Q\) and gives
\[
A_Pg_Q=b_P,\qquad \theta(Q)=R_Pg_Q.
\]
Thus, on the single event \(P\in\mathcal C_n^P\), every element of \(\Theta_I(P)\), simultaneously over all compatible \(Q\), belongs to \(\mathcal C_n^\theta\).  Binary outcomes imply each contrast lies in \([-1,1]\), so the final intersection does not remove it.  Combining this deterministic inclusion with (2) proves
\[
\Pr_P\{\Theta_I(P)\subseteq\mathcal C_n^\theta\}\ge1-\alpha
\]
at every rank and without rank selection.

It remains to make termination explicit.  Write a trial table as \(p_e(a,y,x,w,z)\), and set
\[
q_e(x,z,w)=\sum_{a,y}p_e(a,y,x,w,z),\qquad
m_e(x,z)=2\sum_w\{p_e(r_e,1,x,w,z)-p_e(l_e,1,x,w,z)\}.
\]
Every candidate complete cell is at least \(\eta>0\), so \(q_e(x,z)=\sum_wq_e(x,z,w)>0\).  Multiplying the conditional bridge equation by this denominator gives the equivalent polynomial equation
\[
\sum_wq_e(x,z,w)
\{g_{r_e}(w,x)-g_{l_e}(w,x)\}=m_e(x,z).
\tag{3}
\]
Known balanced randomization is expressed by
\[
\sum_yp_e(a,y,x,w,z)=\frac12q_e(x,z,w),
\]
and target integration by
\[
\vartheta_a=\sum_{x,w}p_0(x,w)g_a(w,x).
\tag{4}
\]
Normalization, cell lower bounds, (3), (4), and the binomial-tail inequalities defining \(B_n\) are finitely many polynomial equalities and weak or strict inequalities in \((p,g,\vartheta)\), of finite degree.  After multiplying the tail inequalities by \(2M_{\mathrm{total}}\), one may retain \(\alpha\) and \(\eta\) as free variables, so all polynomial coefficients in the input formula are rational binomial coefficients.  Consequently membership of \(\vartheta\) in \(\mathcal C_n^\theta\) is a finite existential first-order formula over a real closed field.  The cited effective real-closed-field quantifier-elimination theorem terminates on this formula and returns an equivalent quantifier-free semialgebraic description.  No bound on \(g\), denominator inversion, or rank choice is introduced.

added_lemmas.statement:
For a matroid on a finite ground set \(E\) with rank function \(r_M\), the rank of the union of \(q\) copies is
\[
r_{M^{\vee q}}(E)=\min_{F\subseteq E}\{|E\setminus F|+q\,r_M(F)\}.
\]
For the graphic matroid, \(r_M(F)=|V|-c(F)\).

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(M\) have rank \(r\), let its smallest nonzero singular value be at least \(\kappa>0\), and retain singular values above \(\kappa/2\).  In a sufficiently small neighborhood, this truncated Moore--Penrose map is smooth at \(M\), singular values obey the operator-norm perturbation bound, and its derivative in direction \(E\) is
\[
D(M^+)[E]=-M^+EM^++M^+M^{+\mathsf T}E^{\mathsf T}(I-MM^+)
+(I-M^+M)E^{\mathsf T}M^{+\mathsf T}M^+.
\]

Applied after the attainable-row theorem and the tree-packing criterion of \cite{NashWilliams1961}, its disjoint-forest and minimizing-set outputs certify whether the causal operator can generically attain rank \(q(|V|-1)\); no new combinatorial min--max theorem is claimed.

proposed.statement: Fix a stratum of common-proxy rank \(q\).  If the candidate menu contains a set \(F\) with \(r_q(E\cup F)=q(|V|-1)\), then adding the minimum-cost set \(F_*\) makes \(A_{P,x}\) attain rank \(q(|V|-1)\) for almost every attainable row collection.  If this saturation holds in every stratum, then \(\ker(A_P)\subseteq\ker(R_0)\), so all target root contrasts \(\theta\) are generically identified for every compatible target latent mixture.  Every feasible augmentation uses at least \(q(|V|-1)-r_q(E)\) new labeled trial edges in the fixed stratum, and equality holds whenever the menu contains an extension of a maximum union-independent set.  If no such \(F\) exists, no choice of trials from the menu can remove the corresponding generic causal rank deficit.

open_obligations.what_is_open: Whether annihilation of every fixed-completion two-sided support-face tangent space is sufficient for global point identification across all compatible latent representations.
open_obligations.obstruction: The support-face calculation is local and fixes a latent representation, whereas the compatible full-data fiber may have disconnected components with different proxy kernels, latent factorizations, or outcome support faces. No frozen assumption gives path connectedness or a theorem reducing global secants to local tangents.
open_obligations.attempted: The support-restricted signed-array equations were derived without division by proxy-kernel entries and both directions of the fixed-representation tangent characterization were checked. The remaining promotion was tested by a path-integration argument, which stops precisely because paths between arbitrary compatible completions are not guaranteed.
open_obligations.partial_result:
For a fixed compatible completion \(Q\), an exact computable local characterization is available.  Let \(\mathcal N_Q^{\pm}\) be the set of bridge increments \(h\), with \(h_0=0\), for which there are signed arrays \(\xi_{s,x,u,w}\) supported on \(\mathcal Y^+_{s,x,u,w}\) such that
\[
\sum_y\xi_{s,x,u,w}(y)=0,\qquad
d_{s,a}(x,u,w):=\sum_y\xi_{s,x,u,w}(y)y_a,
\]
and the following finite linear equations hold:
\[
\sum_u Q(U=u\mid Z_e=z,X=x,S=e)C_x(w\mid u)d_{e,a}(x,u,w)=0
\]
for every trial \(e\), assigned endpoint \(a\in\{l_e,r_e\}\), \(x,z,w\), and
\[
\sum_wC_x(w\mid u)\{d_{s,a}(x,u,w)-d_{s,0}(x,u,w)\}
=\sum_wC_x(w\mid u)h_a(w,x)
\]
for every \(s,x,u,a\).  These equations are well defined even when \(C_x(w\mid u)=0\), and support feasibility is computed by the range of the restricted marginal map \(\mathscr L_{s,x,u,w}\).  The set \(\mathcal N_Q^{\pm}\) is a linear subspace obtained by Gaussian elimination.  Every \(h\in\mathcal N_Q^{\pm}\) yields, for all sufficiently small positive and negative \(\varepsilon\), the kernels \(K+\varepsilon\xi\), which preserve every observed cell and the shared latent contrasts and change the target by \(\varepsilon R_0h\).  Conversely, differentiating any two-sided fixed-support perturbation that keeps the latent mixtures, proxy kernels, and assignment mechanism fixed gives exactly these equations.  Thus the fixed-\(Q\) locally attainable target-direction space is \(R_0\mathcal N_Q^{\pm}\), and local point identification along this route is equivalent to \(R_0\mathcal N_Q^{\pm}=\{0\}\).  What is not closed is the promotion of this local, fixed-representation criterion to global point identification over all compatible latent representations and disconnected support faces.
